name: Interaction Patterns
description: Governs all interaction patterns, component states (hover, active, disabled, loading, empty, error), navigation models, gestural interactions, and cognitive-perceptual constraints like Fitts's Law and Hick's Law. Use this skill whenever the user asks about interactive states, loading screens, empty states, error handling, confirmations, modals, button sizes, touch targets, chunking, or animation. Trigger for any UI review focusing on how components behave when interacted with.

rules.rule: Make primary interactive targets large and place them close to the user's natural starting cursor/thumb position.
rules.why: The time required to rapidly move to a target area is a function of the ratio between the distance to the target and the width of the target.
rules.check: Is the primary action the largest and most easily reachable target on the screen?
rules.bad: A tiny 16x16px "Save" icon placed in the far top-right corner of a dense form.
rules.good: A large, full-width "Submit" button placed immediately below the final input field.

rules.rule: Never use the distinction between red and green as the sole indicator of system state.
rules.why: Red-green color blindness is the most common form of color vision deficiency. Blue and orange is a much safer oppositional pairing.
rules.check: If you render the screen in grayscale, can you still tell the success state from the error state?
rules.bad: A system status dashboard where online servers are marked with a green dot and offline servers with a red dot, with no o
rules.good: Online servers have a green checkmark icon; offline servers have a red warning triangle icon.

rules.rule: Limit the number of presented options at any given time to avoid overwhelming the user (Hick's Law).
rules.why: The time it takes to make a decision increases logarithmically with the number of choices. More options often lead to choice paralysis.
rules.check: Could this list of options be categorized, chunked, or reduced without losing core functionality?
rules.bad: A main navigation menu with 40 flat links all exposed simultaneously.
rules.good: A navigation menu with 5 top-level categories, each revealing its specific links only upon interaction.

rules.rule: Group related items into chunks of 4±1 to accommodate the strict limits of human working memory.
rules.why: The brain can reliably hold about 4 items in active memory at once; chunking allows the brain to process larger amounts of information by remembering the chunks instead of the individual pieces.
rules.check: Are long lists or numbers broken into smaller, easily digestible groups?
rules.bad: Displaying a 16-digit credit card number as a single continuous string: `4111222233334444`.
rules.good: Displaying a credit card number in chunks of four: `4111 2222 3333 4444`.

rules.rule: Use animation only to draw attention to critical state changes, establish spatial relationships, or provide feedback—never for mere decoration.
rules.why: The human visual system is biologically wired to immediately focus on motion in the periphery. Gratuitous animation creates cognitive fatigue and distraction.
rules.check: If this animation were removed, would the user lose context about what just happened in the interface?
rules.bad: A dashboard where every widget bounces and fades in slowly upon page load, distracting the user from their actual data.
rules.good: A newly added item in a list briefly flashes a subtle background color so the user knows exactly where it appeared.

rules.rule: Provide an "Undo" mechanism for all destructive or complex actions rather than relying solely on confirmation dialogs.
rules.why: The cost of an error is proportional to the effort required to fix it. "Undo" provides a safety net that encourages exploration and reduces anxiety.
rules.check: If the user accidentally clicks the primary action, can they reverse it with a single click?
rules.bad: Deleting an email instantly removes it forever without any way to recover it.
rules.good: Deleting an email removes it from the list and shows a temporary toast notification with an "Undo" button.

rules.rule: Every interactive element must have explicitly designed normal, hover, active (pressed), and disabled states.
rules.why: Missing states break the affordance feedback loop, leaving users uncertain if the system registered their intent.
rules.check: If I mouse over, click, and disable this component, does it visually change every time?
rules.bad: A button that looks the same whether it is enabled or disabled, relying on an error message to explain why it won't clic
rules.good: A button that dims and drops its shadow when disabled, darkens on hover, and visually depresses on click.

rules.rule: Use skeleton screens (placeholder UI) instead of loading spinners when the structure of the incoming data is predictable.
rules.why: Skeleton screens reduce perceived loading time by providing an immediate structural mental model, whereas spinners draw attention to the delay.
rules.check: Do you know the layout of the content that is currently loading?
rules.bad: Showing a single, tiny spinning circle in the center of the page while a complex dashboard layout loads.
rules.good: Showing a grayed-out wireframe representation of the text blocks and images that are about to populate the screen.

rules.rule: Use loading spinners or progress bars for actions where the outcome is not a new visual layout (e.g., submitting a form, uploading a file).
rules.why: When the layout isn't changing, the user just needs to know that the system is actively working on their request.
rules.check: Is the system performing an action rather than fetching a new view?
rules.bad: Freezing the UI with no feedback while a 5MB file uploads.
rules.good: Replacing the "Submit" button text with a spinner and the word "Uploading..."

rules.rule: Never show a blank screen or a simple "No data" message for an empty state. Always explain what goes here and provide a clear primary action to populate it.
rules.why: The first-run empty state is the prime opportunity to set the user's mental model of what the feature does.
rules.check: Does the empty state tell the user exactly what to do next to make the screen useful?
rules.bad: A saved items page that just says "0 Items Found" in the center of the screen.
rules.good: A saved items page showing an illustration, the text "You haven't saved any articles yet", and a "Browse Articles" butto

rules.rule: Error messages must explicitly state what happened, why it happened (if helpful), and the exact action required to fix it.
rules.why: Reporting an error without a solution creates a dead end, punishing the user.
rules.check: Can the user read the error message and immediately know exactly what they must type or click to resolve the issue?
rules.bad: "Form submission failed. Error Code: 400."
rules.good: "We couldn't process your payment because the card has expired. Please update your expiration date or use a different ca

rules.rule: Use modal dialogs strictly for critical actions that require the user's explicit attention before the system can proceed.
rules.why: Modals are hostile interruptions that break the user's flow. They should be reserved for irreversible actions or systemic blockages.
rules.check: If the user ignores this message, will the system break or will data be permanently lost?
rules.bad: Using a modal dialog to show a non-critical marketing announcement or a "Successfully saved" confirmation.
rules.good: Using a modal dialog to confirm the deletion of an entire project repository.

rules.rule: For highly destructive actions, require the user to explicitly acknowledge the specific consequence, not just click "Yes" or "OK".
rules.why: Users quickly learn to blindly click "OK" on standard confirmation dialogs without reading them (habituation).
rules.check: Does the confirmation dialog require the user to read the button text to know what they are confirming?
rules.bad: A dialog asking "Are you sure you want to delete this?" with the buttons "Cancel" and "OK".
rules.good: A dialog asking "Delete the project 'Alpha'?" with the buttons "Keep Project" and "Delete Project".

rules.rule: In dialogs or forms, visually differentiate the primary action (commit) from the secondary action (cancel) using distinct weights.
rules.why: Two buttons of equal visual weight require the user to stop and read both to avoid making a mistake.
rules.check: If you blurred the screen, could you still tell which button moves the process forward?
rules.bad: A form with two identical blue buttons side-by-side: "Submit" and "Cancel".
rules.good: A form where "Submit" is a solid blue button, and "Cancel" is a borderless, gray text link.

rules.rule: Use standard gestural patterns (swipe to delete, pinch to zoom) only where users natively expect them, and provide visible alternatives.
rules.why: Gestures are inherently invisible affordances; if a user doesn't know the gesture exists, the feature is inaccessible.
rules.check: Is there a visible button or menu option that accomplishes the same task as the hidden gesture?
rules.bad: An email app where the *only* way to delete an email is to swipe left, with no delete button on the screen.
rules.good: An email app that allows swiping left to delete, but also provides a visible "Edit" mode with explicit delete buttons.

rules.rule: Elements that support drag-and-drop must feature explicit drag affordances (like a grip icon) separate from their clickable areas.
rules.why: Mixing click and drag on the exact same surface creates ambiguity and frustrating mis-clicks.
rules.check: Does the user know exactly where to click to drag the element versus where to click to open it?
rules.bad: A list item where clicking anywhere opens the detail view, but clicking and dragging anywhere also reorders the list.
rules.good: A list item where the main body opens the detail view, and a distinct "six-dot" grip icon on the left edge is used exclu

rules.rule: Use flat navigation (e.g., bottom tab bars) rather than hierarchical navigation (e.g., deep menus) when users need to rapidly switch between core views.
rules.why: Hierarchical navigation requires high interaction cost (backing out, opening menus, finding new targets) compared to the single-tap cost of a flat navigation bar.
rules.check: Do users need to frequently alternate between these two views in a single session?
rules.bad: Placing the user's "Inbox" and "Calendar" inside a deep hamburger menu that requires 3 taps to switch between.
rules.good: A bottom navigation bar with "Inbox" and "Calendar" icons, allowing 1-tap switching.

rules.rule: Allow users to edit data in the context of its display (in-place editing) rather than navigating them to a separate "Edit" page.
rules.why: Taking users away from the context of their data forces them to memorize the context, increasing cognitive load.
rules.check: Can the user see the surrounding data while editing this specific field?
rules.bad: Clicking an item in a list navigates the user to a completely new screen just to change the item's title.
rules.good: Clicking the title of an item transforms the text into an input field right where it is.

rules.rule: When an item is selected from a group, its selected state must be unambiguously distinct from the normal and hover states of the unselected items.
rules.why: Users must be able to glance at a list or navigation bar and immediately know their current location or selection.
rules.check: Is the selected state visually distinct enough that it cannot be confused with a hover state?
rules.bad: The selected navigation tab is slightly darker gray, while hovering over an unselected tab makes it the exact same dark
rules.good: The selected navigation tab has a bold font, a distinct brand-colored background, and a strong underline, completely unl

rules.rule: Any operation taking longer than 1 second requires a progress indicator; anything longer than 10 seconds requires a determinate progress bar and an option to cancel.
rules.why: Users perceive delays longer than 1 second as a system failure unless told otherwise. Delays over 10 seconds break the user's attention span.
rules.check: Does the user know roughly how much longer they have to wait for this operation to complete?
rules.bad: An indeterminate spinning icon for a database migration that takes 3 minutes.
rules.good: A determinate progress bar showing "45% complete (Estimated time: 2 mins)" with a "Cancel Migration" button.

rules.rule: Ensure the keyboard focus state (tabbing) is visually distinct from the mouse hover state to support accessibility and varied input modes.
rules.why: Focus states serve users navigating via keyboard, while hover states serve pointer devices. Conflating them can confuse keyboard users about where their focus actually lies.
rules.check: If you tab to a button, does it look specifically focused (e.g., an outline) rather than just hovered?
rules.bad: Using `outline: none` for keyboard focus, relying entirely on a subtle background color change shared with the hover sta
rules.good: A button that darkens on hover, but gains a prominent 2px blue focus ring when navigated to via the keyboard.

rules.rule: Accept data in whatever reasonable format the user provides, and let the system do the work of formatting it.
rules.why: Forcing users to translate their mental model of data (e.g., a phone number with parentheses) into the system's arbitrary format (e.g., strictly numbers) creates unnecessary friction and errors.
rules.check: Does the system reject common, human-readable formats for standard data types?
rules.bad: Rejecting a phone number because the user typed `(555) 123-4567` instead of `5551234567`.
rules.good: Accepting `(555) 123-4567` and having the application strip the formatting behind the scenes before saving.  ## Anti-pat
